events.title: JavaScript ES6 standardized
events.summary: On June 17, 2015, the ES6 standard was adopted — adding classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, and block-scoped variables to JavaScript.
events.about: ES6 (also called ES2015) modernized JavaScript for large apps: `import`/`export` for splitting code into files, `class` syntax, arrow functions, promises for async work, and `let`/`const` instead of leaky `var`. It made building React-scale frontends and Node.js services feel like a modern language instead of a hack.

narrative.whyChosen: ES6 was the biggest JavaScript update since 1999 — the release that made modern frontend frameworks possible.
narrative.whyImportant: Developers finally got modules, classes, and proper scoping that other languages had had for years — without giving up JavaScript's ubiquity in the browser.
narrative.problemSolved: JavaScript felt stuck in the 1990s for large codebases; teams were bolting on workarounds until the language itself caught up.

events.title: Swift 2 announced at WWDC
events.summary: Apple announced Swift 2 at WWDC on June 8, 2015 with error handling (`try`/`catch`), protocol extensions, and availability checks.
events.about: Swift 2 made the language feel production-ready: `guard`, improved error propagation, and `@available` for API versioning. Apple also previewed open-sourcing Swift — setting up the December 2015 release that expanded beyond iOS.

narrative.whyChosen: Swift 2 added the error-handling and API patterns iOS developers needed daily.
narrative.whyImportant: It bridged Swift 1 experiments to the open-source Swift 2.x line.
narrative.problemSolved: Swift 1 lacked robust error handling and protocol-oriented patterns for large apps.

events.title: Open Container Initiative launched
events.summary: Docker, CoreOS, and others launched the OCI on June 22, 2015 — an open standard for container image formats and runtimes, donating runc as the reference implementation.
events.about: OCI specs define how container images are built, stored, and executed — image manifest, runtime bundle, and registry distribution. runc implements the runtime spec; containerd, CRI-O, and Podman build on it. Example: a `docker pull` image conforms to OCI Image Format; `runc run` starts it per OCI Runtime Spec.

narrative.whyChosen: OCI prevented container formats from fragmenting into incompatible vendor silos.
narrative.whyImportant: It let Kubernetes, Podman, and Docker share images and runtime semantics.
narrative.problemSolved: The container ecosystem needed vendor-neutral standards before proprietary formats locked in users.

events.title: CockroachDB open sourced
events.summary: Cockroach Labs launched CockroachDB as open source on June 4, 2015 — a distributed SQL database inspired by Google Spanner.
events.about: CockroachDB spreads PostgreSQL-compatible tables across nodes with serializable transactions and automatic failover — survive zone or region outages without manual failover scripts. Ex-Googlers Spencer Kimball, Peter Mattis, and Ben Darnell built it after leaving Viewfinder. It targets cloud-native apps that need SQL semantics with horizontal scale beyond single-node Postgres.

narrative.whyChosen: CockroachDB brought Spanner-style distributed SQL to the open-source world.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved strongly consistent SQL could scale across datacenters without giving up ACID transactions.
narrative.problemSolved: Teams outgrew single-node Postgres but needed SQL, not the tradeoffs of eventual-consistency NoSQL.
